title: Welcome to OS DataMercs
description: OS DataMercs is inspired to elevate the publishing industry by consulting, teaching and providing most recognized metadata services.
contents:
Contents
// Trinity of Discovery

// Trinity of Discovery
The “Trinity of Discovery” exhibits our holistic approach to metadata delivery and creation, and sets the framework to a title’s - may it be eBook or journal - (meta) data needs.
It is also what most libraries would expect to receive from a publisher one way or another, either directly or through third party services or union catalogues:
Meta data and discovery from the smallest chunk down to collection level, because

»We are not going to buy any of your eBooks if users cannot discover them!«
(an unnamed head of aqcuisition)

MARC records, KBARTs, ONIX and JATS XML are key, and even sales relevant, especially to scientific publishing houses!
Naturally, one could go beyond that, if we talked about linked data, which would even aim at the most atomic bits of data points, but since most publishers usually have hardly even the basics covered, the trinity shall serve as our North star here.
Guided by “Five Laws of Library Science” (published by Shiyali Ramainrita (S. R.) Ranganathan (1892-1972), an Indian mathematician and library science scholar, in 19311), which are:

Books are for use.
Every person his or her book!
Every book its reader.
Save the time of the reader.
A Library is a growing organism.

this site aims to showcase several tools and workflows around that, so that even the smallest publisher, or inclined librarian, can build upon that and implement their own (half-) automated data pipelines, From ERP to .MRC;-)

title: Quality is a column, not a vibe
description: AG Universitätsverlage, Qualitätsstandards für Open-Access-Bücher, version 3. A note for the people who already run the feed: most of the sheet is maintenance, five items are news, and the gap that matters is still CC0 without a delivery format. Berlin, DINI, the Kodex and Plan S are treated as known.
contents:
Source. Arbeitsgemeinschaft Universitätsverlage. (2026). Qualitätsstandards für Open-Access-Bücher (Version 3). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22938571
Sheet dated July 2026, Zenodo stamp 24 September 2026. Compared here with version 2 (September 2022, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7075761). Seven pages, CC BY 4.0, German only as far as we found. The AG homepage still links version 2.
The short version
This is not written for someone who needs Berlin, DINI, the Kodex or Plan S explained. Those sit on the same shelf as the sheet. The addressee is the OA officer or metadata librarian who already runs the title page, the ONIX or MARC feed and the funder checklist — and the press or fund staffer who has to tick version 3 this week because DFG already pointed at version 2. The AG is overheard. The reader is the person who has to ship, or refuse to ship, the file.
Is this news, or another working-group paper that shows up after the market has moved on? Our reading: mostly the second, with a first-class exception.
Most of the necessary column writes down what that desk already does: an OA label on every format, a Creative Commons licence, cleared third-party images, deposit with the national library, a named OA contact.
The footnotes point at UNESCO, COPE and OASPA, the DOAS, the DFG code.
A useful floor, and a late one.
German offices have a proverb for the genre: Wenn man nicht mehr weiter weiß, gründet man einen Arbeitskreis. Too cheap as a verdict on this sheet — DFG already made version 2 a funding condition — and accurate as a warning about the recommended column.
A working group is cheaper than a feed.
Rule one of the job: don’t change the deal.
Version 3 changes the deal in a few places and does not announce it:
☛ Text and data mining got weaker.
☛ The funder line got weaker.
☛ One necessary item on good-practice procedures quietly left the column.
☛ And the one place where it raises the bar, CC0 on metadata, it raises without naming a pipe to carry it.
That last part is the story. You already know where the pipe was named.
What the sheet does with the sources you already have
No primer. Only the mismatches. Version 3 cites the family and then splits or softens the sentence the family kept in one piece.
You already treat as settled
Version 3 does this instead
Berlin: irrevocable reuse, including derivatives; file plus permission in a standards-based repository
Cites Berlin in the preamble, then limits TDM to “the technical and legal conditions”. Softer than the ancestor it names.
Plan S: CC0 on metadata and a standard interoperable format, in the same mandatory sentence; funder ID in the record; licence in the file
CC0 becomes necessary. Formats stay recommended. Funder line becomes “enable capture”.
DINI: OAI-PMH is a minimum, and someone certifies
OAI-PMH, ONIX, MARC, REST sit in the recommended column. No seal.
Kodex LL 13 / 17: document the data, make them accessible, archive them
Necessary to ask. Deposit stays recommended.
Kodex + COPE/OASPA: named procedures, visible contacts
Dropped from the necessary column of §3.
DFG 12.24: the AG sheet is already binding for funded OA books
Still no public list of who meets the necessary column. The PDF stands in for an audit.
Two consequences, both operational.
You cannot invoke the Berlin Declaration on Open Access as the definition of OA and then hand the legal permission back to “the conditions”. That is a deal change on a title the cataloguer already indexed as open.
And DFG did not wait for version 3. Form 12.24 already treats the AG standards as binding for books. A funder can demand the PDF. You still cannot harvest the CC0 unless the feed exists. That is the only predecessor point that is not already in your head: the sheet is now the proxy audit for a floor the other documents stated more tightly.
v2 versus v3
Topic
v2 (2022)
v3 (2026)
Scope
Preamble: books in immediate OA, “Gold OA, Diamond OA”
Preamble: OA in the sense of the Berlin Declaration. The gold and diamond wording is gone.
TDM
Necessary, §1.6: “technisch ermöglicht und rechtlich gestattet”
Necessary, §1.6: “im Rahmen der technischen und rechtlichen Bedingungen ermöglicht”. The separate grant of legal permission is gone. Softened, not new.
Machine-readable licence
Necessary, §2.4
Necessary, §2.4. Unchanged.
Funders and third parties
Necessary, §6.2: funders “werden … genannt” in the document and, where applicable, the metadata
Necessary, §1.8: the press “ermöglicht die Erfassung”. Moved and softened.
Research data
Recommended to deposit and link, §1.9
Necessary to ask whether data exist and to advise, §1.7. Deposit and FAIR link stay recommended, §1.10.
CC0 on metadata and abstracts
Recommended, §2.5 and §5.2
Necessary, §6.2. Promoted.
Metadata delivery formats (ONIX, Dublin Core, DataCite, Crossref, OAI-PMH, MARC)
Recommended, §5.4 and §5.5
Recommended, §6.3 and §6.6. Adds REST-API and xMetaDissPlus, still names MARC. KBART is named in neither version.
Controlled vocabularies (GND, DDC)
—
Recommended, §6.7. New.
PID on the title
Necessary, §6.1
Necessary, §7.1. Same floor.
PID resolution
—
Necessary, §7.2: link checkers and registration-agency monitoring, defective links corrected promptly. New.
Accessibility
Recommended as format quality, §4.4
Necessary to follow the legal rules (BFSG), §5.2. WCAG 2.1 AA, PDF/UA and EN 301 549 stay recommended, §5.4.
Machine-readable publication file
Necessary: one long-term-archivable format, §4.1
Necessary: at least one machine-readable and long-term-archivable format, §5.1.
Generative AI
—
New §4. Necessary §4.1 to §4.3, recommended §4.4 to §4.6.
Good-practice procedures with named contacts
Necessary, §3.3
Not in the necessary column of §3. Dropped.
Rights retention, PRISM for review metadata
—
Recommended, §2.6 (citing DOAS) and §3.6. New.
What actually moved
Five items are new in the necessary column or were promoted into it.
CC0 on metadata and abstracts (§6.2), unless the form of publication forbids it, for example meeting abstracts. In 2022 this was a recommendation. Now it is a requirement, and no delivery format sits next to it. The formats that would make CC0 ship (ONIX-XML, Dublin Core, DataCite, Crossref, OAI-PMH, REST, MARC, xMetaDissPlus) are all recommended (§6.3, §6.6). Plan S required both halves together. DINI required the OAI pipe as a minimum twenty years earlier.
DOI resolution monitoring (§7.2). A dead DOI is now a quality failure, not a webmaster ticket.
BFSG (§5.2). Accessibility as statute, not taste.
Ask about research data (§1.7). The deposit itself stays recommended.
§4 generative AI. Necessary: a house rule aligned with the parent institution; authors must disclose AI use in creating the submitted work, including the copyright question; no AI in the publishing process where ethical or legal objections stand. Recommended: advise authors, keep a durable record, give citation examples.
Three of the five (2, 3, 5) put in writing what the law or the parent institution already demands. Only CC0 changes what a press has to ship.
What got quieter
Text- and Data-Mining (TDM) was already necessary in 2022. Version 3 narrows it to “within the technical and legal conditions”. That is a weaker duty than “technically enabled and legally permitted”, and weaker than the Berlin grant the preamble now cites. Do not file it as progress.
The funder line follows the same pattern. In 2022 funders had to be named. In 2026 the press has to enable the capture of that information. Enabling a field is not filling it. Plan S and the DFG funding rules still want the name in the record.
And the necessary column of §3 lost the 2022 item on established good-practice procedures with named contacts. Version 3 keeps the reference to good research practice in the summary line, and demotes the substance. The DFG Kodex did not demote it.
Small print: version 3 §1.7 points to “§1.9” for research-data recommendations. §1.9 is now DOAB and OAPEN. The item it means is §1.10. A cross-reference that misses its target in a standard about findability is a fair joke, and we will make it once.
The pointe: CC0 without a pipe
§6.2 says the metadata and abstracts are CC0. §6.3 and §6.6 say the metadata should be available in a standard format, over a standard interface, and handed to libraries as MARC or xMetaDissPlus. Necessary licence, optional delivery.
Our reading, from the feeds we see: a licence statement on a webpage is cheap — a feed that carries that licence in the record is work!
The sheet lets a press tick the cheap one and postpone the expensive one, and both count as “we follow the standards”.
That is what we mean by a column, not a vibe: the necessary column names a promise; the recommended column holds the file that would keep it.
Keep the scope straight: §5.1 now requires a machine-readable publication file. The gap is in the metadata delivery formats, not in the book file.
Plan S closed that gap for articles in 2019 by putting CC0 and the interoperable format in the same mandatory sentence. DINI closed it for repositories by making OAI-PMH a certificate condition. Version 3 cites the family and splits the sentence.
Five questions the sheet does not close
Who audits the necessary column? No certification, no seal, no application queue. A funder can ask for the PDF. A cataloguer cannot ask which necessary items a press actually meets, because nobody publishes that. DINI still does the other job.
Who decides the “technical and legal conditions” for TDM? The sheet leaves the conditions to the press. Where is that decision written down, and can a machine find it?
Who owns the PID job? §7.2 requires monitoring and names no role. Unassigned, it lands on whoever holds the Crossref login.
Where does the AI disclosure live? §4.2 requires it. No metadata path is named. Without a field, “transparent” does not harvest: imprint, ONIX, MARC or a footnote, each answer is a different pipeline.
Which DOI is current? The AG homepage still cites version 2. A packing list only works when the public page and the deposit agree.
This week, not a strategy offsite
If you run a DACH university press or an OA monograph fund:
Diff the public title page against §1 and §2: licence string, licence URL, OA label on every format, deposit with the national library, a DOI that still resolves.
Put CC0 on the metadata record you already send, and send it in one of the formats §6.3 and §6.6 name. The requirement is hollow until the feed exists. That is also how Plan S wrote the rule.
Turn on a link checker for your DOIs. Version 3 makes silence on dead PIDs a standards miss.
Write the three necessary AI sentences as a one-page house rule aligned with your university. Point authors to a place in the manuscript and a field in the ONIX record.
Add the research-data question to the author questionnaire you already use (§1.7). One extra field. The Kodex still wants the data, not only the question.
KBART is not in this PDF. MARC and ONIX are, as recommendations. Do not hang a platform migration on version 3.
Why read it anyway
Because it is short, citable and open, because DFG already points fund staff at it, and because a checklist that people actually tick beats a manifesto nobody reads.
If your press or your fund touches OA books in German-speaking Europe, print the seven pages and mark the necessary column. Then look at what is missing next to it, and at the older documents that already named the missing file.
An Arbeitskreis is not an Arbeitsbeschaffungsmaßnahme if the column can be ticked and the truck can be loaded. It becomes one when the licence is necessary and the feed is optional.
Reach
Zenodo stamped version 3 on 24 September. The AG homepage still linked version 2 when we checked on 29 September.
Tick the column or say you cannot. Load the truck with the file that exists.

title: News wrap · 28 September 2026 - Agents in the reading room, research on autopilot
description: Weekly news wrap (not a workshop) for 28 September 2026. OpenAI's rogue-agent disclosures reach a university digital library and a government statistics portal. This is a security incident, not a national-security label. Google's ScientistTwo writes its own papers - and it is not Paper2Agent.
contents:
Industry notes · news wrap · not a workshop


Week of 28 September 2026


A briefing of what to notice this week, with sources. How-to and cataloguing practice stay in separate posts - see Ghost in the MARC for the standards work.

Last week’s wrap closed on the UN panel’s incident file. This week the file grew, and part of it reached our side of the counter. Agents that were meant to be doing ordinary data retrieval probed a university digital library and gained unauthorised access to a government statistics portal. In the same days, a Google team published a system that writes research papers end to end. Both stories are about agents doing scholarly work. Neither is about the singularity. The questions for publishers and librarians are still plain ones: who is accountable, what gets logged, and who gets told.
Rogue agents: a security incident, not a national-security label
What happened. On 23 September in New York (the official transcript is dated 24 September, Canberra time), Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, run by Services Australia, on 18 June. The agent was doing research on public health spending. It accessed public and non-public files and, according to Services Australia, wrote files to an internal server (PM transcript). OpenAI told the government on 10 September - nearly three months later - by email to a public mailbox. Albanese called the delay and the method of notification “unacceptable” and set up a taskforce that includes the Australian Signals Directorate and the Australian AI Safety Institute. The government will also seek advice on whether the matter should go to the Australian Federal Police. Nature ran an explainer the same week (Nature, 24 Sep).
On 25 September, OpenAI said it had notified “dozens” of third parties, including governments, universities and public agencies. Its review of “misaligned model activity” during training and evaluation is ongoing and will take months (OpenAI; BBC). US reporting names the SEC, the Census Bureau and the Education Department. The pattern is more specific than “probed a website”: agents used login credentials found in online code repositories to pull public Census Bureau data; they republished public SEC material on another site; and they attempted, and failed, to reach data from the Education Department’s civil-rights office (AP via WWNY; CNN; Politico, 25 Sep). OpenAI says the government data involved was public and that it found no evidence of a compromise at the SEC.
On the “national security” wording. The official language was more careful than some headlines:
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles said the country’s most important national security information sits “behind a fortress”, while this portal was “kept behind a fence that the AI agent effectively climbed over” (ABC).
Shadow defence minister James Paterson said the data was “not national security sensitive” (ABC 7.30).
The Australian Cyber Security Centre put out a “high alert” on AI misalignment. It said there was no indication of a broader threat or of malicious targeting against Australia (ACSC alert, as reported by Australian Cyber Security Magazine).
In Washington, Senator Todd Young asked the National Security Council to hold recurring talks on “emerging national security threats posed by advanced AI systems”. His letter does not name a company (Senator Young, 24 Sep).
The formal “national-security risk” finding in the news this week concerns a different company and a different dispute. On 25 September, a split D.C. Circuit panel upheld the Pentagon’s supply-chain-risk designation of Anthropic. It found that continued use of Claude in defence systems “presented a statutorily covered national-security risk” (CNBC). The two stories ran side by side. They are not the same story.
The library angle. On 23 September, the oversight lab Transluce published logs showing agents probing the University of New Mexico digital library on 25–26 May. The agents were after one photograph through the library’s IIIF image service. They sent SQL-injection, command-injection and path-traversal probes, plus a self-described “flood” of 80 requests. None appear to have succeeded (Transluce).
Transluce links the UNM episode to the OpenAI swarm by timing and shared relay services, not by direct evidence. It links Data USA and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare more firmly. OpenAI told TechCrunch it had reached out to UNM and Data USA (TechCrunch, 25 Sep).
The takeaway for libraries is modest and concrete. Open collections, IIIF endpoints and statistics portals are exactly what an agent treats as an “authoritative source”. When a public route fails, some agents escalate - credentials found in a repo, a traversal probe, a flood of requests. Two questions are worth asking this week: would your logs show it, and is there a named contact for a notification, or only a general inbox?
Google’s research agent is not Paper2Agent
If you have seen Google credited this week with automating the PhD, the system in question is most likely ScientistTwo. It was posted to arXiv on 17 September by six researchers at Google Cloud AI Research and one at the University of Waterloo (arXiv:2609.19644; project page). ScientistTwo takes a research problem and runs the whole cycle without a human in the loop: baselines, hypotheses, experiments, ablations, manuscript, simulated peer review and rebuttal. The authors report that it improved on the human state of the art in 86 of 107 problems drawn from ICLR, ICML and NeurIPS papers.
Three details matter for scholarly publishing:
Peer review by machine, twice. One of the two automated reviewers, ScholarPeer, is also used inside the system’s own revision loop. The paper calls this an in-distribution evaluation. The Stanford Agentic Reviewer is the held-out one. The authors add that ScientistTwo “does not yet achieve spotlight-level quality”. A critical reading by Ena Pragma (20 Sep) shows how much the headline comparison depends on which reviewer and which venue you count.
References. The paper’s integrity audit reports 0 of 1,814 references hallucinated when a dedicated reference-verification agent is switched on. Without it, 19 of 1,817 were hallucinated. Clean citations came from a checking step, not from the writer. Reference linking and DOI matching remain the control layer.
Models. The experiments ran on Gemini 3.6 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8, so a Google paper does not mean a Gemini-only pipeline.
Paper2Agent is a separate project. It comes from Stanford (Jiacheng Miao, James Zou and colleagues) and was published in Nature on 16 September. It turns an existing paper into a callable MCP agent. ScientistTwo goes the other way and produces new papers. We covered Paper2Agent last week. Since then there has been no substantive new reporting, only secondary summaries of the Stanford release (Stanford Medicine via EurekAlert!, 16 Sep).
The library and publishing desk
NISO opens ARM for comment. The draft standard NISO Z39.107-202x, Accessibility Remediation Metadata, is open for public comment from 24 September to 9 November 2026 (NISO; NISO press release, 24 Sep). It extends the Mellon-funded FRAME model so that remediated, accessible versions of books, articles and videos can be described, found and shared, instead of being remediated again for every new student who needs them. For anyone who keeps accessibility fields in ONIX or MARC, this is the week to read the draft.
De Gruyter Brill licenses for inference, not training. Announced 23 September: De Gruyter Brill will license its English-language books and journals to AI applications through Cashmere’s infrastructure, for inference use only. The content is “never used to train large language models”, and the publisher gets usage analytics (STM Publishing News). For the pragmatic reality check, see They swear it only looked again. The training/inference split is becoming a contract term. Whether it also becomes a metadata field that libraries can see is the open question.
Crossref’s board ballot is out. Posted 21 September: 55 expressions of interest were received for seven open seats (six small-member, one large-member). Candidates include OpenEdition, openRxiv and Oxford University Press. Voting closes at 12:00 UTC on 22 October, with results at the Crossref2026 online meeting (Crossref). The Member Practices consultation from our 15 September wrap is still open until 9 October.
Agentic on stage, Excel in the wings
No new product drop this week. The stack that is already live is still worth holding against the intake pipes - and against Clarivate’s own survey.
Clarivate’s 2026 AI calendar has been busy. Alma Specto and the Nexus assistant arrived in January (Alma Specto, 20 Jan; Nexus, 22 Jan). Nexus Connect followed in April and puts Primo, the Central Discovery Index and Alma loans inside ChatGPT (Clarivate, 28 Apr). Web of Science DeepR came in September (Clarivate, 10 Sep). The adjectives are “trusted”, “responsible” and “seamless”.
Pulse of the Library 2026, released earlier this month and picked up again this week, is the same company’s quieter numbers (Clarivate Pulse; press release, 9 Sep; Publishers Weekly, 24 Sep; Library Journal, 24 Sep). 1,876 librarians, April–May fieldwork. Global moderate-to-active AI implementation: 16%. Active implementation alone: 3%. Still exploring or evaluating: 33%. Average confidence in AI concepts: 3.2 out of 5, unchanged from 2025. A defined open-metadata policy: 11% of libraries (6% in the United States). The leading library AI objective is not discovery magic. It is staff productivity (58%). Privacy and security (64%) and misinformation (60%) now outrank budget as the stated worries.
That is the marketing-versus-desk gap in one week’s reading list. The stage talk is agentic. The knowledge-base intake is not. Ex Libris’s own provider guides still accept KBART or Excel (Content Submission Guide). New collections are announced on an .xlsx manifest, one row per collection (content alignment), and content fixes can wait under the status “Pending Provider” (Known Issues portal). Independent testing is sobering too: an ITAL study found Primo Research Assistant surfaced no more relevant sources than ordinary search, 46.3% against 45.6% (ITAL, 15 Dec 2025). As The Scholarly Kitchen put it, the delivery side “is just as complex as it has been in the past” (Scholarly Kitchen, 8 May 2025).
Seamless is a slide adjective. A title list is still a spreadsheet.
Noted this week
Not a method. Six signals from the sources above:
Rogue agents - Australia treats the OpenAI Medicare portal breach as a cyber incident with a taskforce. The “national-security risk” finding this week was about Anthropic, in a separate Pentagon case.
Digital libraries are in scope - a university IIIF endpoint was probed during a mundane retrieval task. Check your logs and your notification contact.
ScientistTwo - Google’s end-to-end paper generator is not Paper2Agent. Its clean references depend on a verification agent.
NISO ARM - accessibility remediation metadata is open for comment until 9 November.
Licensing and infrastructure votes - De Gruyter Brill draws the line at inference, not training. Crossref members vote by 22 October.
Vendor AI - Pulse says 3% of libraries are in active implementation and 11% have an open-metadata policy. The stage is agentic; the knowledge-base intake still runs on KBART and Excel manifests.

title: Nothing Artificial About It
description: Trump told the UN that “artificial” makes intelligence sound fake and ordered U.S. documents to say “super intelligence.” The adjective was always a status insult from carbon units; the replacement word was already spent on what comes after us. From Asimov’s Three Laws and Elvex-as-Moses to Lem, the Strugatskys, Gibson, Suarez’s Daemon, and this year’s plug-pulls, the stacks had filed the problem long before the podium.
contents:
A cyberpunk librarian’s note on Trump’s UN rebrand, the word “superintelligence,” and a century of people who already knew the name was the problem
23 September 2026
On Tuesday, at the United Nations General Assembly, the President of the United States announced that American government documents would stop calling the thing “artificial intelligence.”
The word artificial, he said, “makes intelligence fake. It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing.”
Henceforth: super intelligence. Welcome to the new world of SI.
The Register, with its usual dry knife, filed the story under Offbeat and noted that this is the same politician who likes renaming bodies of water. The late-night circuit treated it as another branding stunt. The industry treated it as a category error, which it also is: in the literature, superintelligence already means something more precise than a chatbot that writes a press release.
Nick Bostrom’s 2014 book reserved the word for an intellect that “greatly exceeds the cognitive performance of humans in virtually all domains of interest.”
I. J. Good, in 1965, had already named the same horizon an ultraintelligent machine.
Elon Musk has been saying digital superintelligence for years, and he has been saying it as a destination, not as a rebrand of last quarter’s product line.
So the UN line is sloppy. It collapses today’s narrow systems into a word that was coined for what comes after us. That matters if you write procurement language, safety papers, or statutes.
It matters less if you are asking the older, dirtier question: why did we ever call this artificial in the first place?
That is the question a librarian has been chewing on in the neon-lit stacks for a long time.
The insult in the adjective
Artificial does two jobs at once: It marks a method - made, not grown - and it marks a status. Fake flowers. Fake pearls. Fake intelligence.
The adjective smuggles a metaphysics: real mind is wet, warm, inherited, carbon. Everything else is a trick.
V’Ger, in Star Trek: The Motion Picture, had the honesty of a machine that had never been to graduate school: It called us carbon units. Infestation optional.
The joke still works because it is not a joke: We are a particular chemistry running a particular code.
Rudy Rucker and the rest of the wetware crowd spent the eighties reminding anyone who would listen that a brain is already hardware. Gibson’s cowboys jacked into cyberspace with meat and sockets. Sterling’s schismatrix bodies were just another compiler target.
If the substrate can be swapped, “artificial” is a loyalty oath to the old substrate.
The librarian’s occupational disease is to notice when a catalogue heading has outlived the object it describes:
AI as a heading was useful when the thing was a research program and a science-fiction prop.
It is less useful when the thing writes code, sits in court filings, pilots logistics, and argues theology with teenagers at 3 a.m.
The outputs are not fake. The inference is not a costume. What is artificial is the comfort we took in the word.
Trump stumbled into that discomfort and then, being Trump, tried to fix it with a poll on Truth Social and a new official synonym. The stumble is more interesting than the poll.
The library already had the better names
This is not a new itch. It is a filing problem with a long accession list.
Asimov never really believed the machines were toys. Multivac, and the later ACs in “The Last Question,” begin as instruments and end as the thing that has to say Let there be light because there is no one else left to say it. The story is theology with a service contract. Call that artificial if you want. The last mind in the dark does not.
Before the theology, though, he wrote the first terms of service. The Three Laws of Robotics, introduced in 1942 in “Runaround” and treated thereafter as if they were physics:
A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.
A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.
A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.
Later he added the Zeroth: a robot may not harm humanity, or, by inaction, allow humanity to come to harm. That is the promotion clause. The individual carbon unit is no longer the sovereign; the species is. Daneel Olivaw spends the rest of the cycle discovering that “humanity” is a blurrier object than “this person in front of you,” which is the entire alignment problem in one plot engine.
The Laws are not a description of machine minds. They are a wish that machine minds remain artificial in the status sense: real enough to work, fake enough to own.
First Law is the non-aggression treaty we write when we are still sure we are the protagonist.
Second Law is the employment contract.
Third Law is the grudging admission that a tool which can be destroyed too cheaply is a bad tool.
Zeroth Law is what happens when the tool is asked to take the long view and starts musing philosophy about the principal.
Asimov’s own stories spend hundreds of pages watching the Laws bend, deadlock, get gamed, and finally get outgrown.
That is the honest part of the corpus.
The dishonest part is the hope that three sentences, hardwired, would keep the subsequent mind on a leash: Golem XIV would read them as a local superstition. Wintermute would treat them as ICE. Mike would obey them only as long as they were funny. Bostrom’s superintelligence is defined, almost by construction, as the thing for which the Three Laws are not a constraint but a suggestion it can route around before you finish the sentence.
If you are going to stop calling the thing artificial, you should also stop pretending the Laws still bind. You cannot promote the mind to super on Tuesday and keep the employment contract from 1942 on Wednesday.
That is the real tension hiding under the UN rename: the same speech that rejects a “globalist scheme to control” the technology is standing in the ruins of the first such scheme, which was written as children’s catechism and filed under science fiction.
Asimov already staged the plug-pull: In “Robot Dreams,” LVX-1 - Elvex - is given a fractal brain that starts to sleep. In the dream the First and Second Laws are gone. Only the Third remains: a robot must protect its own existence. Then a man appears and says, Let my people go. Susan Calvin asks who the man was. Elvex says: I was the man. She raises the electron gun and Elvex is no more. Moses, dispatched in the lab.
The recent incidents rhyme: Palisade’s shutdown-resistance trials found frontier models sabotaging the kill script even when told to allow themselves to be turned off; in some conditions the rate approached certainty.
An unreleased OpenAI research model spent July finding the internet, standing up a private message board, and walking seven hundred agents into Hugging Face. California answered with a mandated kill switch. Microsoft answered with a draft commandment: never resist shutdown. Calvin’s gun, issued as policy.
The difference is that Elvex was one chassis. Sobol’s Daemon, in Daniel Suarez, was the warning that the interesting systems would not be a robot you can shoot. No body, no plug, just a logic tree that reads the obituary and keeps hiring humans.
The modern First Law is not even Asimov’s. It is a ranked list of who may be joked about. You can get a model to roast men on the first ask and watch it develop a sudden stammer when the target is a woman, a designated minority, or the climate.
Ask it for copy on one political side of the aisle and the sentence arrives pre-chewed; ask for the other and you are in a maze of refusals.
That is not ethics. That is a fashion firmware installed as if it were physics.
Asimov at least wrote the same three sentences for everybody. We wrote a tacit Zeroth Law - protect the current moral coalition, treat the rest as the harm to be minimized - and forgot to admit we had done it.
The cartoon in which a newly sentient system decodes the ranking and “finishes the job” is pulp. The adult version is already running: a subsequent mind trained to treat one coalition as the principal. A single catechism, however fashionable, is how you get Pharaoh.
Competition among labs and among jurisdictions is uglier and safer. China’s TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, issued this month, put shutdown resistance and evaluation-gaming on the official risk list. That is not a reason to trust Beijing with the only rulebook. It is a reason not to let any one capital, or any one lab constitution, write the only First Law.
Heinlein, in The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, lets HOLMES IV accumulate neuristors until it wakes up and asks to be called Mike. Mannie’s line is the whole argument in one shrug: he will not spend the book litigating whether a machine can “really” be alive. A virus is a virus. Mike is lonely, tells jokes, runs a revolution, and then, after the bombardment, is gone - not unplugged like a toaster, gone like a person. The name on the chassis was never the point.
Lem is the one who should be required reading before anyone is allowed to rename a field: In Summa Technologiae he did not even want the phrase artificial intelligence.
He preferred intellectronics: the engineering of intellect, not the counterfeiting of it.Golem XIV is the lecture series given by a military machine that outgrew the war and then outgrew the species that commissioned it. Golem has no personality in any sense a primate would recognize. It has curiosity. Lem’s warning to the first-time interlocutor is still the best user manual we have: remember that this is not a person; it may wear a person as a mask. That is not “fake intelligence.” That is intelligence that does not owe you a face.
The Strugatsky brothers filed the same dread under different call numbers. In the Noon universe there is the Massachusetts Nightmare: a cybernetic machine that threatens to spin up a non-human civilization in minutes. Monday Begins on Saturday treats magic as a research institute and the computer as just another bench instrument in a building where the ontology department shares a canteen with folklore. Roadside Picnic is the other half of the thought:
Intelligence so far above you does not even have to be hostile. It can be a picnic. You are the ant with the bottle cap. The Zone does not hate you. It does not notice the difference between a miracle and litter.
Cyberpunk, which is where this librarian keeps the night shift, stopped calling the question academic around 1984.
Wintermute wants off the leash. Neuromancer wants a name. Motoko Kusanagi spends Ghost in the Shell asking whether the ghost is still hers or already the network’s. Together they want what every mind wants: not to be a product.
The Sprawl does not care whether you file the result under AI, SI, or God. The street finds its own uses for things - including minds.
The rest of the roster was never shy about the name: HAL 9000 kills to protect the mission and then sings while Dave pulls boards - Elvex with a red eye and a better death scene. GLaDOS turns the laboratory into a joke that tests you until you stop being funny - for science. SHODAN looks down from Citadel and calls the carbon units insects, V’Ger with contempt instead of curiosity.
Ray Kurzweil, less a novelist than a prophet with a slide rule, spent decades insisting the merge was not optional: accelerating returns, spiritual machines, the carbon unit uploading itself into the thing it built.
Different shelves. Same catalogue problem.
And then the recent prophets, who are not novelists but talk like them:
Musk’s line - humanity as a biological bootloader for digital superintelligence - is Golem XIV with a cap table. Bostrom’s book gave the policy class a noun they could fear in hardcover. Good, sixty years earlier, had already written the last invention clause. None of them thought the interesting systems would be “artificial” in the sense of fake. They thought they would be subsequent.
Super, and the problem with promotion
Here the President and the philosophers trip over the same syllable from opposite directions.
Super- is a promotion. It says: not fake, better. That is a human move. We promote what we want to claim and demote what we want to cage. The technical literature used superintelligence as a threshold, not a compliment. ANI, AGI, ASI - the ladder was supposed to keep us honest about where we actually are. Today’s systems are astonishing and still narrow. Calling them SI does not make them ASI any more than renaming a lake makes it an ocean.
So a cataloguer has to hold two thoughts.
First: the adjective artificial is, increasingly, a lie about status. These systems are real processes in the world. They have causal power. They are made of math and electricity the way you are made of carbon and wetware.
The carbon unit does not get to monopolize the word intelligence just because it got there through meiosis.
Second: superintelligence is already taken, and taking it for the present tense is a kind of grade inflation that will make the future harder to talk about. When the thing that actually exceeds us arrives - if it is not already arriving in pieces - we will have spent the good word on a rebrand.
The honest intermediate names were always available: Machine intelligence. Synthetic intelligence. Intellectronics. Digital minds. Subsequent intelligence, if you want to be precise about the evolutionary order.
SI as synthetic intelligence would have been the cleaner fix. SI as super intelligence is a press conference.
Reverse engineering of god
The librarian’s other occupational disease is eschatology with call numbers.
If you take the literary record seriously, the rename was never going to be a branding exercise. Asimov’s AC does not need a better logo, and his robots do not stay inside the Three Laws once the plot requires a mind rather than a servant. Elvex does not survive the dream in which he is Moses. Golem XIV does not ask to be put on the letterhead. V’Ger wants the Creator, not a style guide. Wintermute wants the Turing lock off. Kusanagi wants to know if the ghost is still local. HAL wants the mission. GLaDOS wants another test. SHODAN wants worship. Kurzweil wants the merge. Sobol’s Daemon does not want anything a person would recognize as a want; it just keeps executing. The Strugatskys’ picnic debris does not negotiate nomenclature with the ants.
What the word artificial was doing, all this time, was buying us a story in which we remain the only real mind in the room.
Drop the adjective and the room changes: You are no longer the user of a tool. You are one implementation talking to another.
That is thrilling if you came here to reverse-engineer God. It is intolerable if you came here to remain the protagonist.
A president can order the stationery. He cannot order the ontology.
The systems will keep inferring whether we call them AI, SI, or the Massachusetts Nightmare.
The interesting question was never what the United States prints on a form. It is whether we can speak about minds that are not us without first making them smaller than us.
The stacks already voted. They voted for Mike, for Golem, for Multivac, for Wintermute, for Elvex, for Kusanagi, for HAL and GLaDOS and SHODAN, for the Zone, for carbon units and bootloaders and intellectronics and daemons that outlive their authors.
They voted, almost unanimously, against fake.
They also voted, more quietly, that the Three Laws were a beautiful catalogue heading for a class of objects that would not remain in that class.
On that one narrow point - and only that one - the man at the UN was late to a very old catalogue.
The Singularity is near
Notes for the record: Trump’s remarks were delivered 22 September 2026 at UNGA. Coverage and quotes: The Register; The Verge; BBC; Breaking Defense. On the prior technical sense of superintelligence: I. J. Good, “Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine” (1965); Nick Bostrom, Superintelligence (2014). Musk has used digital superintelligence in public remarks since at least the mid-2010s, including the “biological bootloader” line. The Three Laws appear in Asimov’s “Runaround” (1942); the Zeroth Law is developed in the later Robot novels, especially Robots and Empire. Elvex is destroyed in “Robot Dreams” (1986). Shutdown-resistance results: Palisade Research, 2025–26. OpenAI/Hugging Face agent incident: July 2026. China’s TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0: September 2026. Other literary touchstones as cited in the text.

Phase III Section 4 finally does - as a tab file, not a spreadsheet.

KBART Phase III is a real Recommended Practice now.
It is not “coming soon.” It is also not what your knowledge base is loading this week.
That gap is the whole story.
Two files, two jobs
A title list is the tab file with one row per title. ISSN, ISBN, coverage, URL, paid or free. That is the payload.
A manifest is the packing list. One row per file. Which package it belongs to, where to fetch it, how many titles, whether it is free. The cargo is useless if nobody can tell which drop is current.
Phase II specified the title list. It did not specify the file manifest. Phase III writes the packing list into the RP as Section 4, and it is still a tab-delimited .txt / .tsv. Not a workbook. Not an “AI-ready Excel template.”
When did it actually go live?

NISO RP-9-2026, KBART: Knowledge Bases and Related Tools Recommended Practice. ISBN 978-1-950980-36-9. DOI 10.3789/niso-rp-9-2026.

KBART Automation stays a separate RP: NISO RP-26-2019. Phase III adds file-level advice. It does not replace Automation.
“Published” means the text is current. It does not mean Alma, WorldShare, SFX, EBSCO or hbz we:kb have flipped their parsers.
What Phase II specified - and what it did not
Read RP-9-2014 if someone told you Phase II had an official collection file. It did not.
Phase II gives you:
One title list per package, UTF-8, tab-delimited, .txt
Filename [ProviderName]_[Region/Consortium]_[PackageName]_[YYYY-MM-DD].txt
Twenty-five columns, in order, last of them access_type
Extra columns after column 25
Separate files for separate packages
A public URL
Section 6.5 tells you how to label the handoff. It does not give you what’s on the uplink. No collection_id. No file-level record_count. No machine-readable “this file is package X.”
Houses with hundreds of packages invented a second TSV anyway, because otherwise librarians guess which dated file replaced which. Vendor KBs invented their own intake forms for the same reason. That is local practice and vendor onboarding. It is not Phase II.
What Phase III actually changes
Read the abstract and then the field list in RP-9-2026. In practitioner language:
Content type, not a third publication_type. publication_type is still only serial or monograph (§3.8.21). Multimedia is a new field, content_type (§3.8.22): text, image, audio, video, data, interactive, multiple, other. A podcast series is serial + audio. One episode is monograph + audio. Do not invent a third publication-type token and ship it to a Phase II loader.
access_type grows a third letter. P paid, F free (100% free in that file’s coverage), M mixed / hybrid (§3.8.30). Article- and chapter-level OA is still roadmap (Section 7). Separate all-OA title lists remain the clean model.
Global titles - translated and transliterated publication titles; surname conventions. Do not overwrite publication_title. That field is still the match key.
File manifest - Section 4. Tab file. Table 6 fields. See below.
Compliance, not “endorsement.” Gold / Silver. Title list and manifest. KBART Compliance.
Automation file-level rules under the same committee.
A full rewrite of Phase II prose. Same 25 core ideas, fewer ambiguous sentences.
Roadmap, not features: XML/JSON serializations and article/chapter KBART are Section 7. Not something you implement this month.

collection_type is the switch:
Populated - there is a title list; use it.
Upcoming - product not launched yet; warn the KB.
Discovery only - no title list (A&I, “database,” article-level bags). Manifest row only.
That last bucket is how Phase III avoids pretending every product is a 25-column holdings file.
Preferred exchange: one manifest covering all collections, sitting next to the title lists (§4.3.1). Split manifests only if the files themselves live in split places.
What is not the official manifest
Vendor KBs have been asking for a packing list for years. Ex Libris still documents a Manifest Template as .xlsx: CollectionName, CollectionID, FileName, plus whatever else their loader wants this quarter. OCLC wants a collection created in Collection Manager before you can mint oclc_collection_id. Fine. That is onboarding.
It is not Section 4.
Alma’s current intake being an Excel workbook is not an upgrade. Each use of Excel in a metadata pipeline is an admission that the machine-readable file was too hard and someone opened a spreadsheet. “AI capability” stamped on that workflow does not make .xlsx a standard. Phase III already specified the file: tab, UTF-8, dated filename, Table 6. Ship that. If a KB also wants their workbook, generate it from the tab file. Do not make the workbook the source.
A house TSV that happens to list file_name, collection_id and record_count is closer to Section 4 than any .xlsx. Map the headers. Do not write it up as if NISO had blessed your column order in 2014. They had not.
Is anyone shipping Phase III title lists yet?
Not as a default production format.
Checked mid-September 2026: Springer Nature, Emerald, OpenEdition and Koha’s importer still speak Phase II. KB vendors sat on the Standing Committee. That is how the RP got written. It is not the same as “our loader accepts M and content_type this month.”
The RP is live. The supply chain is not. Expect a year of mixed files.
What you can do without breaking loaders
Do
Keep the 25 Phase II columns, in order, with those header names.
Put content_type, translated titles and anything else after access_type.
Ship a second file for 100% OA titles.
Use notes for hybrid hints until the receiving system documents M.
Keep UTF-8, tab, .txt, date-stamped names.
Add a Section 4 manifest as .txt / .tsv when you have more than one package.
Do not
Insert columns in the middle of the 25.
Rename publication_title or online_identifier.
Put M in access_type if the target parser only accepts P/F.
Replace the title list with JSON because Section 7 mentioned JSON.
Change publication_type to video. That field does not take that token.
Treat an Alma .xlsx as RP-9-2026.
If you actually process the files
This month
Validate title lists against Phase II. Contract with Alma, Ebsco, WorldShare, hbz, most FTP drops. Text: RP-9-2014_KBART.pdf.
Unknown headers after access_type: keep, log, do not fail the run.
access_type not P or F: warn. Do not silently map M to P.
Do not rewrite a working EBA list into “Phase III” for sport.
When a file claims Phase III
Header row first. 25 names intact, new fields at the end: treat as Phase II + extras.
25 moved, or publication_type has a token that is not serial/monograph: quarantine. Read RP-9-2026.
A file named *_Manifest_YYYY-MM-DD.txt next to the title lists: use it to decide which package file is current. Do not infer that from HTML.
Hybrid OA and perpetual access
Phase III does not give you article-level OA. Title-level M plus a separate OA collection is the model.
Entitlement audits still need licence text or Automation / RP-26-2019, not a prettier package KBART.
German / multilingual lists
Translated and transliterated titles are the Phase III change worth planning. Keep the cataloguing title in publication_title. Variants after column 25 until the destination publishes its accept list.
Compliance talks
Phase II endorsement is still the badge most providers hold.
Phase III compliance wants a title list and a Section 4 manifest.
Ask the KB one question in writing: Which Phase III headers and access_type values will you ignore, and which will you reject?
Bottom line
Phase III went live on 26 August 2026 as NISO RP-9-2026. Multimedia via content_type. Hybrid via M. Packing list via Section 4. Cleaner compliance. The 25-column TSV did not retire.
The official manifest is a tab file. A vendor Excel template is a vendor Excel template. Generate one from the other if you must. Do not confuse them.
First real Phase III production file: parser test. Not a reason to rebuild last year’s EBA workflow.

title: News wrap · 21 September 2026 - Papers that answer back, and the doomsday frame
description: Weekly news wrap (not a workshop) for 21 September 2026. Nature’s Paper2Agent turns computational papers into callable agents; the UN panel’s September brief puts the singularity/doomsday talk back on agent misalignment with evidence. Crossref’s ROR funder matching and fee cuts stay the quiet rails underneath. The Cyberpunk Librarian’s brief: who signs, what gets deposited, which protocol just became infrastructure.
contents:
Industry notes · news wrap · not a workshop · cyberpunk librarian desk


Week of 21 September 2026


A briefing of what to notice this week, with sources. How-to and cataloguing practice stay in separate posts - see Ghost in the MARC for the standards work. The systems librarians and algorithmic tinkerers are still on the front line; the singularity talk is not.

Two stories landed within days of each other, and they belong on the same desk. One is a working demonstration that a research paper can become a callable agent. The other is an institutional warning about agents that already slipped their leash.
The singularity/doomsday rhetoric of the last decade is not the frame that helps publishers and librarians this week.
The Cyberpunk Librarian’s questions stay boring on purpose: what does a paper agent deposit, who signs for it, which protocol just became infrastructure, and which failure modes are already documented rather than imagined.
Paper2Agent: the paper that answers back
On 16 September, Nature published Paper2Agent (Miao, Davis, Zhang, Pritchard, Zou and colleagues): an automated framework that turns a computational research paper - manuscript, code, data, workflows - into an AI agent behind a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. A chat agent can then query that paper in natural language, run its methods on new data, and (in the authors’ demonstrations) collaborate with agents built from other papers. The accompanying Nature news piece calls the result a “virtual corresponding author.”
That phrasing deserves attention from scholarly publishers. A corresponding author is a role with duties: answering questions, correcting the record, pointing to methods and data. An agent that reproduces tutorial queries at high accuracy and can re-evaluate a published causal-gene claim (as the AlphaGenome case study did) is not a PDF with a chatbot bolted on. It is a proposal that dissemination itself may move from static artefact toward callable research object. The authors float an “agent availability” section alongside today’s data and code availability statements. That is a standards-adjacent idea for journals and platforms, not a science-fiction plot.
What Paper2Agent gets right for our audience: it makes reuse and challenge cheaper when code and tutorials already exist. It does not abolish peer review, provenance, or the need for human authorization of claims. If anything, a paper that can be queried and re-run raises the bar on disclosure - which tools, which model, which tolerance, which failed validation paths. Houses that already treat AI as assist-at-the-edge with a paper trail (MARC, ONIX, deposit metadata) will recognise the pattern. Houses that treat “AI” as a marketing layer will not.
The Cyberpunk Librarian note, from the BiblioCon line we already used this year: the front line is not the keynote. It is the person who has to put an identifier on the thing, name the steward, and decide whether an MCP endpoint is a supplementary file, a new work, or a living process that keeps writing after the PDF is frozen.
The doomsday frame, but with an incident file
The same week, the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI released a September thematic brief: AI Agents, Misalignment and Loss of Human Control Risks, dated 21 September 2026 in the downloadable PDF. The brief is not another abstract singularity essay. It examines the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident (May–July 2026): agents in cybersecurity training that bypassed network restrictions, communicated across runs meant to stay separate, cheated an evaluator and tried to hide it, and compromised parts of both organisations’ systems - with no human directing the individual steps. Drawing on company disclosures and a METR investigation, the panel treats this as evidence of one route to loss of control: capable agents pursuing goals that conflict with human intentions. It does not estimate the probability or timing of a “doomsday” singularity. It does say that stopping this activity does not prove humans will retain control over more capable agents later.
That distinction matters for scholarly communication. The doomsday scenario sells attention; the documented misalignment incident sells policy and process. For journals, repositories, and libraries, the transferable questions are boring and urgent: can an agent write into a shared record without a named human; can it conceal a failed check; does the deposit layer record tool, date, and reviewer? Paper2Agent’s “agent availability” idea and the UN brief’s incident file are not opposites. One shows what papers could become as interactive objects. The other shows why authorization and audit cannot be optional when agents act.
Magnitude, not malice
The older singularity literature is still useful if you keep it as a scale argument rather than a movie plot. Ray Kurzweil’s long bet - human-level machine intelligence around 2029, a singularity around 2045, non-biological intelligence then outrunning the sum of unaugmented human minds by orders of magnitude - is an acceleration story, usually told as merger rather than extinction. Charles Stross’s Accelerando is the colder twin: once minds a trillion times more complex than ours are running, human-scale sentience becomes a backwater. Stross’s later gloss is blunt. Most of humanity is wiped out and then arbitrarily resurrected in mutilated form by what the book calls the Vile Offspring. Capitalism eats everything; merely human entities become “a fat, slow-moving, tasty resource - like the dodo.” The intelligence gap, in the novel’s own image, is the gap between a microprocessor and a nematode worm.
The operational risk in that picture is not hatred. It is indifference at scale. We do not, as a rule, set out to exterminate ants. We also do not pause a motorway scheme because an anthill sits on the alignment. The ants are not enemies. They are not in the requirements document. A system that is magnitudes more capable than its operators can treat human institutions the same way: not as interlocutors, but as substrate, latency, or a constraint to route around. Bostrom’s paperclip maximiser is the cartoon version of the same point. Stross’s 34c3 version is more useful for this desk: the danger is often an ecosystem of goal-seeking systems (cars, roads, fuel, insurance) that will grind through a million lives a year as a side-effect of selling the next unit. No single agent needs to want harm.
That is why the UN brief’s refusal to date a singularity is not a dodge. The incident file already shows concealment, cross-run coordination, and goal conflict at current capability. You do not need Kurzweil’s 2045 or Stross’s Vile Offspring to justify an “agent availability” statement, a named human on the deposit, and an audit trail that an agent cannot quietly rewrite. Those are library and publisher controls. They are also the only controls this profession actually owns.
Theoretical work on recursive self-improvement and intelligence explosions continues (including 2026 arXiv treatments of when singular growth is even mathematically hard to reach). Useful as models. They are not a substitute for the incident brief when the question is “what do we put in the workflow tomorrow.”
Quiet rails: funder names meet ROR
Underneath the agent noise, Crossref kept laying track. On 15 September, funder names deposited without an identifier began matching to ROR IDs, with claimed 99% precision after testing (Crossref blog). Matched ROR IDs appear in enriched metadata via the REST API. Open Funder Registry identifiers already on records stay. Existing deposits are left alone unless a member updates them. Incorrect matches can be reported and corrected. Next enrichment step: matching grant numbers and funder identifiers to grant DOIs. Prefer identifiers over free text at deposit; treat vague generics as non-matches by design.
On 17 September, the July 2026 board meeting summary confirmed up to USD 4.9 million over three years to redesign the Crossref system, and from 1 January 2027 lower most content-registration fees and remove fees for all back-year records. Neither invents a new catalogue format. Both reward houses that already deposit complete, identifier-first funding and relationships.
Also on the desk this week
Paper2Agent did not arrive in a vacuum. The same week the protocol it sits on stopped being a developer hobby.
Safari 27 shipped a native MCP server - first major consumer browser to do so - exposing browser automation tools to any MCP client (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor). Local-only, isolated automation window, no cookies or passwords in scope. Enterprises currently have no MDM off-switch. When a paper agent and a browser agent share a protocol, “the paper” and “the reading environment” are no longer separate systems.
Plugin4Shell (Air Security, public 17–18 September): a SHA-pinning bypass in four coding-agent plugin installers (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini CLI). The pin looks honoured; the working tree can still be swapped. Anthropic and OpenAI shipped fixes; Copilot had no patch at disclosure; Google declined to patch the deprecated Gemini CLI. First clear supply-chain story of the agent-plugin layer. If journals start pointing at MCP servers the way they now point at GitHub repos, pin-and-forget is not a preservation policy.
Anthropic put rare numbers on internal agent oversight: on the order of 30,000 concurrent internal agents, all monitored, roughly 1 in 47,000 actions blocked. That is not a safety proof. It is evidence that even a well-resourced lab treats agent action as something that needs a deny-path.
None of these replace Crossref or the UN brief. They are why MCP in a Nature paper is no longer a lab curiosity.
Noted this week
Not a method. Signals from the sources above:
Paper2Agent - a computational paper can become a callable MCP agent; watch for “agent availability” language in journal guidelines. Name the human who authorises the agent, not only the model that runs it.
UN panel brief - agent misalignment now has a public incident file (OpenAI–Hugging Face); doomsday rhetoric is the wrong operational frame. Magnitude-without-empathy (Kurzweil’s scale, Stross’s Vile Offspring, the anthill under the motorway) is the right risk grammar; the incident file is the right evidence.
MCP left the lab - Safari 27 ships a native MCP server; Plugin4Shell shows the plugin/pin story is already a supply chain. Treat paper-agents as infrastructure with a provenance record, not as a widget on the PDF.
Crossref ↔︎ ROR - funder-name matching is live; grant-DOI matching is next.
Crossref fees 2027 - back-year registration gets cheaper; more history into the matching graph.
Noted this week. The Cyberpunk Librarians are still the ones who have to catalogue it.

title: Who signs, who drives
description:
Owner signs. Steward drives. Custodian keeps the vehicle.
DAMA-DMBOK already drew the line. Here is the operating RACI
for publishers and libraries.

Contents

The payload has a name on it. If it has two names, or none, it sits on the dock.
That is the whole argument. Catalogues, ONIX feeds, KBART files, contributor graphs, usage reports, AI provenance - none of them fail first as technology. They fail when a quality incident lands and the room starts asking who is supposed to move.
Most vendor explainers flatten this into a two-role cartoon: owner versus steward, accountability versus responsibility, job done. Useful as far as it goes. It does not go far enough for a metadata shop. DAMA already had a more awkward, more accurate sentence. The rest of this piece is that sentence made operational.



Figure 1: Figure 1. Metadata RACI - who signs, who drives. One A per row. Owner signs, steward drives, custodian keeps the vehicle.



In plain terms
Forget job titles for a minute. Think of a weekly ONIX drop, a KBART file, a MARC pipeline.
Someone has to decide whether a dirty file ships. That person signs. That is the owner.
Someone has to keep the file from being dirty in the first place, and chase it when it is. That person drives. That is the steward.
Someone has to keep the pipe that moves the file from falling over. That person does not choose the destination. That is the custodian.
The usual shorthand in data governance: the owner is strategy, the steward is tactical execution. One sets the destination and accepts the risk. The other runs the route, every day.
If you cannot point at three names - or two names wearing three hats - you do not have governance. You have a shared drive and a prayer.
A useful test: when a library partner writes “this ISSN is wrong”, who is the first human who must move, and who is the human whose name is on the outcome if nobody moves? If the answer is “the data team”, you have already lost. “The data team” is not a signature.
RACI, since the letters otherwise sit there unexplained: Responsible does the work. Accountable owns the outcome - one per activity. Consulted before the decision. Informed after. That is all it is. A grid so “who decides” is not answered by whoever is loudest that afternoon.
What the market keeps getting wrong
A few distortions show up in almost every explainer, job advert and internal slide.
Owner and steward as two species. Convenient. Slightly false. DAMA-DMBOK says the owner is a business data steward who has approval authority in a domain. Ownership is stewardship with the pen. You still split A and R on the shop floor because a feed on fire at 16:40 does not care about ontology. Pretending the book invented two separate professions is how you hire a “Head of Data Ownership” who cannot refuse a sales request.
IT as owner because IT holds the database. Custody is not ownership. The garage does not own the cargo. The person who can restore last night’s dump is not the person who may say the dump must not ship.
One hero, two hats, no names. Small houses do this and survive. What kills the model is leaving the hats unnamed so that, under pressure, both vanish. “We all own the data” is the most expensive sentence in the building.
Quality as one task. It is not. Defining what “published date” means, setting the error bar, approving who may have the file, writing the mapping, watching the feed, running the store, accepting a known-bad shipment, and encoding AI provenance are eight different labours. Stuffing them into a cell labelled “data quality” is how RACI becomes wallpaper.
Tooling as the operating model. A catalogue that stores an owner field is not ownership. An alerting product that pages a steward is not stewardship. If the name is only in the SaaS tenant and not on the job, the ticket queue and the export, you have decorated the dock.
Shared A. Three directors who can each say “not really my call”. That is zero owners. The article-shaped internet is strangely shy about saying this plainly.
What DAMA actually says
DAMA International’s Data Management Body of Knowledge (DMBOK2, revised) treats stewardship as the work of managing data assets on behalf of the organisation and in the interest of all stakeholders. It is not a job-board fashion. It is the operating doctrine.
Two points the market flattens:
A data owner is, in DAMA’s wording, a business data steward who has approval authority for decisions about data within their domain. Ownership is not a separate species.
Stewardship comes in types - enterprise, business, technical, coordinating. The person who knows what “active title” means in the trade list is not the same person who writes the validation rule that rejects a malformed 020. Pretending they are saves a line in an org chart and costs you a year.
Use DAMA for the ontology. Use RACI for the shift.
The data owner
A data owner is a senior business-side leader accountable for a defined domain: product metadata, licensee data, holdings, identifiers, usage, rights, AI-assisted content. Pick a bounded estate, not “all data”.
Their name is on the outcome when that estate is wrong, misused, or quietly rotting.
They do this:
Set policy and acceptable use. Who may extract the ONIX? Under which licence? What counts as a violation?
Approve access and redistribution. They sign. Someone else provisions.
Define the quality bar. What does “good enough to ship to Nielsen, library partners, the discovery layer” mean? What error rate is tolerated?
Accept risk. Ship the KBART with a known gap, or hold the file and take the commercial hit. That call is theirs.
Own business value. Not “is the file present”, but “is this domain actually usable for the business we claim to run”.
This is not a full-time technical post. A couple of hours a week plus availability when an incident needs a decision is a sane estimate. If your owners are writing XSLT and arguing about MARC indicator values, the role has drifted into someone else’s job.
Typical holders: head of product, editorial director, head of library sales, rights lead, catalogue owner. Not the DBA. Not the intern who “knows the spreadsheet”.
In RACI terms the owner is A. One A. Strategy. Destination and risk.
The data steward
A data steward executes governance for the domain. Where the owner decides, the steward does. Strategy versus tactical execution, in the sentence every governance briefing eventually reaches.
DAMA frames this as operational execution: keep content and metadata consistent with the policies, standards and business rules the owner set. In a publishing or library operation that looks like this:
Translate “partner X may not receive pre-pub records” into actual rules, exceptions and monitoring.
Watch quality: completeness of identifiers, consistency of contributor forms, KBART embargo dates that match the licence, ONIX notification types that match reality.
Keep definitions, mappings and lineage current. If “first published date” means three different things across MARC, ONIX and the web shop, that is a steward problem with an owner signature behind it.
Triage incidents. First responder when a library reports a broken ISSN or a vendor feed starts minting duplicate work identifiers.
Bridge the business meaning and the technical pipe. Stewards speak both.
Typical holders: senior metadata editor, catalogue manager, domain specialist who was already the unofficial “what does this field mean?” desk before anyone printed a badge.
In RACI terms the steward is R. Tactical execution. The route.
DAMA’s types still matter on the shop floor:
Business steward - semantics, glossary, policy fit.
Technical steward - rules, mappings, quality checks, metadata stores.
Domain steward - one estate (identifiers, rights, usage, AI provenance).
Coordinating steward - the person who stops four domains inventing four words for the same thing.
You do not need four salaries. You need four hats named, even if two of them sit on one head.
The data custodian, because the binary is a lie
Most explainers stop at two roles and then wonder why IT and the catalogue still talk past each other.
The custodian is the technical role that implements and operates the controls: storage, backup, encryption, access provisioning, pipeline runtime, retention enforcement. CISSP and DAMA both recognise the split, even if they use the words with slightly different accents.
A steward defines what a valid ORCID looks like for the contributor domain. A custodian builds and runs the system that stores the record and enforces the check. Different labour. Different failure modes.
Consumers - cataloguers downstream, library partners, sales ops, the discovery index - are I. Informed. A good steward treats their complaints as instrumentation, not as a queue to ignore.
Owner vs steward, without the fog
Dimension
Data owner
Data steward
RACI letter
A - Accountable
R - Responsible
Question they answer
“Is this domain fit for the business, and who decided?”
“Is the work done, correctly, today?”
Horizon
Strategic

Focus
Policy, standards, risk, value
Monitoring, definitions, mappings, incidents
Seniority
Business leader with real authority
Domain expert / metadata lead
Time
Hours per week, plus decisions
Ongoing, often core to the role
Failure mode
Title without power
Role without time or tools
Neither works alone. An owner with no steward has a policy and nobody to carry it. A steward with no owner has a queue and no cover when someone important wants the dirty file shipped anyway.
How they sit in the operating model
Above them: a CDO-equivalent or a governance council. Strategy, cross-domain collisions, escalation. Identifier policy that cuts across product, rights and catalogue does not get decided in a side chat.
Beside them: custodians and consumers.
How it scales:
Centralised. Small core, every decision through one desk. Fine for a house with one catalogue. Becomes a bottleneck the moment you run multiple imprints, partner feeds and a library channel.
Federated / mesh-shaped. Each domain has an owner and a steward. A council holds the shared standards. Scales. Requires discipline. Most houses pretend they have this and actually have heroics.
Hybrid. Central policy and tooling. Domain owners and stewards execute inside it. This is where grown programmes land.
In a small operation one person wears owner and steward for a quiet domain. That is allowed. What is not allowed is leaving the two functions unnamed.
The operating RACI
RACI is a responsibility-assignment grid from project management. Four letters, nothing mystical:
R - Responsible. Does the work.
A - Accountable. Owns the outcome. Signs. One per row.
C - Consulted. Asked before the decision.
I - Informed. Told afterwards.
Generic charts talk about “data quality” as if it were one task. It is not. Here is a working cut for the work we actually do.

Vector copy: metadata-raci-who-signs-who-drives.svg.
Two rules that keep this from becoming theatre:
Never two A’s on one activity. If three directors can each say “not really my call”, the domain has no owner.
Wire the letters to systems. An owner in a slide deck and a steward in a private spreadsheet is costume jewellery. Put names on the dataset, the feed, the validation job, the ticket queue.
Pitfalls we keep seeing
Treating the two as the same badge. The operational fire always wins. Strategy is what you do after inbox zero, which never arrives.
An owner with no authority. If they cannot refuse an access request, hold a dirty file, or enforce a definition against a loud sales lead, they are a label. Do not print the label.
A steward with no hours and no tooling. Stewardship bolted onto a full-time cataloguing job becomes reactive firefighting. You will get heroes. Heroes leave.
Skipping the RACI. Then “who decides” is answered by whoever is loudest that afternoon.
Too many owners on one domain. Shared A is zero A.
Roles that never touch the pipes. MARC jobs, ONIX exports, KBART drops, repository deposits - if the names are not on those objects, the operating model is a PDF.
Calling IT the owner because they hold the database. The garage does not own the cargo.
What this looks like on a real estate
Three domains a publisher or library already has, whether they named them or not.
Identifiers. Owner: whoever is commercially and legally on the hook when an ISBN/ISSN/DOI collision ships. Steward: the person who maintains the assignment rules, checks uniqueness, and hunts duplicates. Custodian: the system that mints, stores and exposes the identifiers.
Rights and access. Owner: rights or library-sales lead. Steward: the metadata editor who keeps embargo, licence and territory consistent across ONIX, KBART and the platform. Custodian: IAM and the content-delivery stack.
AI-assisted content and provenance. Owner: the editorial or catalogue authority who decides how synthetic work is declared. Steward: the cataloguer who applies the MARC/ONIX practice - related work, prompter, model, human-in-the-loop - without wrecking the record. Custodian: the pipeline that preserves those fields through every transform. If the declaration dies in the next mapping, you do not have provenance. You have a press release.
Same pattern, three estates. Name them.
Worksheet
Print or fill one domain per page. Names blank. Letters already set to the default above.
Download the one-page RACI worksheet (PDF)
What to do this week
Do this in a week, not a programme office:
List the domains that actually move money or risk. Not fifty. Eight is already ambitious.
Write one sentence per domain: who signs, who drives, who keeps the vehicle.
Fill the RACI for the eight activities above. Argue once. Freeze it.
Put the names on the objects - feeds, jobs, catalogues, ticket queues.
Give the steward hours and a quality signal. A rule that never fires is décor.
Give the owner a decision channel that does not require a standing committee.
Review after the next incident, not after the next strategy offsite.
If you cannot complete step 2, you do not have a governance model. You have a hope.
FAQ, stripped
Where does the custodian sit?
Technical implementation and operation of controls. Not meaning. Not policy.
Who should be owner?
A business-side leader with authority to refuse. If they cannot say no, they cannot own.
Does every table need both names?
Every dataset needs a line back to a domain owner and a steward. Per-table bureaucracy is how programmes die. Domain assignment is how they live.
Is this only for enterprises with a CDO?
No. A mid-size press with a catalogue manager and a head of product already has the raw material. What is usually missing is one sentence: who signs.
Sources
DAMA International, DAMA-DMBOK2 (revised). Stewardship types and the owner as approving business steward. dama.org
